items.summary: At Microsoft Ignite 2026, Satya Nadella unveiled Microsoft’s end-to-end "frontier ecosystem" built around three imperatives: keeping humans at the center, enabling organizations to own their intelligence, and establishing verifiable trust.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
At Microsoft Ignite 2026, Satya Nadella unveiled Microsoft’s end-to-end "frontier ecosystem" built around three imperatives: keeping humans at the center, enabling organizations to own their intelligence, and establishing verifiable trust. Key announcements include the broad availability of Work IQ, Copilot Workspaces, Microsoft Decision 1.1, Perception, Horizon DB (integrated into Fabric), Cobalt 200 VMs, and the Microsoft AI Transparency Initiative.

## Copilot & The Multiplayer Workplace
* **Copilot as the Work OS:** Brings together chat, co-work, code, autopilot (24/7 autonomous agents), and all of Office into one experience.
  * **Work IQ:** The underlying organizational database (people, relationships, emails, meetings, chats, projects) is now broadly available.
  * **Role-Based Extensions & Plugins:** New skills, connectors, and business plugins for sales, legal, finance, and service, including **Dynamics 365** and a new partnership with **Salesforce**.
  * **Copilot Workspaces:** A new multiplayer form factor enabling people, their agents, and other teammates to collaborate toward a shared goal with shared context.
* **GitHub Advancements:**
  * **Projects:** Allows developers to define a goal, connect repositories, and have Copilot coordinate task sessions and recurring work.
  * **GitHub Copilot Fusion:** A new composite model family that orchestrates multiple models; ranked #1 coding agent on **Terminal Bench**, scoring **5 points** over **Claude Core** at **less than half the cost**.

## Microsoft IQ, Foundry & The Model Ecosystem
* **Microsoft IQ:** Externalizes the system underneath Copilot as a first-class platform combining Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, Web IQ, and third-party contexts, supported by **hundreds of new connectors**.
* **Microsoft Decision 1.1:** Now generally available with multimodal support, **10x faster** speed, and **200x lower cost** than using an LLM.
  * Already used by **over 4,000 customers**, including **Epic** (patient experience, clinical care, back-office) and **Xbox** (sorting tens of thousands of open-ended game launch feedback items).
* **Foundry Model Additions:** Added **GPT-62** (including **GPT-62 Astra**, which outperformed its predecessor at more than half the estimated cost), **Claude Fable 52**, **Mythos 52**, and **Meta’s** latest models.
* **MAI Model Family & Licensing:**
  * **Momentum:** **MAI Transcribe 2** requests are up **12x** since launching on OpenRouter; **MAI Code Flash** reached **3 million users** on GitHub Copilot last month; **MAI Cyber** powers **over 40%** of scans across Perception code scanning.
  * **New Models:** **Code 2** (flagship agentic coding), **Code 2 Flash** (high-volume tasks), and **Cyber 2 Flash** (integrated with Perception).
  * **MAI Licensed Weights:** Trusted partners can now access Microsoft AI model weights.
  * **Managed Agent Harness:** Foundry now offers the same harness powering Copilot, complete with continuous improvement loops and private benchmarks/evals.

## Trust, Governance & Agentic Security
* **Agent 365:** The enterprise control plane for agent governance, identity, and security already manages **50 million agents**.
  * **Agent 365 Business Analytics:** Newly announced "ERP system of AI usage" to track spend, connect it to business outcomes, and optimize ROI.
* **Perception (Generally Available):** An end-to-end agentic security system combining red team (attack simulation), blue team (detection), and green team (remediation) agents across Entra, MXC, Cloud Containers, Purview, and Defender.
  * In a recent test using the **ArtX** autonomous AI attack framework, Defender’s automated attack disruptions contained compromised accounts and isolated devices at machine speed.
* **Microsoft AI Transparency Initiative:** A three-part effort to establish open, independently verifiable industry standards for AI transparency, security, and governance—already backed by **40 organizations** and being built into MAI models, Foundry, and Copilot.

## Agent-Scale Infrastructure, Data & Silicon
* **GitHub Core Rebuild:** Decoupled storage and compute to handle agentic scale; in testing, **5,000 agents** pointed at one repo sustained **7,200 writes per second** (**180x** current throughput).
* **Azure Scale & Sustainability:** Operates **500+ data centers** across **80 Azure regions**, matching **100%** of annual global electricity consumption with renewable energy and reusing/recycling **92%** of servers and components.
* **Azure Agentic Primitives:** New micro-VMs (sub-1-second startup, full sandboxing, confidential computing enclaves), an agent grid for identity/policy-aware networking, context caching, and AKS / AKS Flex integration.
* **Horizon DB & Fabric Unification:**
  * **Horizon DB:** Distributed managed PostgreSQL database delivering **8x faster** performance than self-managed PostgreSQL, now **generally available** in Azure.
  * **Fabric Integration:** Bringing Horizon DB into Fabric unifies transactional and analytical data, allowing agents and Copilot to reason over live transactions and terabytes of historical records in real time.
* **Custom Silicon:**
  * **Cobalt 200 VMs:** Next-generation general-purpose VMs, now **generally available**.
  * **Maya 300:** Newly announced AI accelerator alongside Azure Boost and Azure Integrated HSM.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Maya 300 Efficiency:** "Maya 300... will deliver over 40% more tokens per watt compared with leading GPU systems." — Satya Nadella
* **Workplace Shift:** "Every function will go through a similar change [to software engineering] across their work, their workflow, and their work artifacts." — Satya Nadella
* **Edge AI Capabilities:** With new Windows PCs, "you can run in some sense last year's frontier models on your laptop and last quarter's models on your desktop." — Satya Nadella

## Notable Quotes
> "AI in the flow of human ambition is perhaps the biggest design challenge we have in front of us." — Satya Nadella

> "It becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it." — Satya Nadella

> "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapse into a couple of models." — Satya Nadella

items.title: Stan Druckenmiller: Why He's "Not Playing" Right Now | TomorrowX Summit
items.summary: After 50 years of investing, Stan Druckenmiller has rarely had less 12-month clarity and has shifted Duquesne Family Office into capital preservation mode ("I'm not playing"), pivoting away from his bullish January positioning as Fed tightening, widening credit spreads, and deteriorating market internals reverse the macro backdrop.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** After 50 years of investing, Stan Druckenmiller has rarely had less 12-month clarity and has shifted Duquesne Family Office into capital preservation mode ("I'm not playing"), pivoting away from his bullish January positioning as Fed tightening, widening credit spreads, and deteriorating market internals reverse the macro backdrop. Looking ahead, he is watching AI use cases—where leading labs sell tasks rather than tokens—and predicts that within 10 years we will see data centers in space, cancer become a managed disease, and a financial-crisis-driven US fiscal reform.

## Why Stan Is "Not Playing" Right Now
* **A Complete Macro Reversal:** In a conversation with Morgan Stanley's Iliana Bouzali—who runs the firm's global derivatives business and hosts macro legend Zoom calls—Druckenmiller noted he owns "almost none" of the bullish portfolio he held in January.
  * **January Backdrop:** Fed funds were at 3.5% against 6% nominal growth, the Fed dot plot signaled rate cuts, credit spreads were tight, commodities (including copper) and the advance-decline line were hitting new highs, and Claude Code had just sparked an AI capex acceleration.
  * **Today's Backdrop:** Everything has flipped. A regime change at the Fed has shifted policy from cutting to hiking after 15 years of free money and 5 years of above-target inflation. Commodities have topped (Duquesne is now short copper), credit spreads are widening, and the advance-decline line peaked on August 14th even as major averages hit highs in October.
* **Capital Preservation Mode:** Druckenmiller is neither long nor short equities—calling his equity book "basically flat" with small positions in the dollar—and refuses to short the market given ongoing AI innovation and washed-out tactical positioning.
  * **Auto-Reply:** Bouzali joked that Druckenmiller now has an auto-reply button that says, "Don't talk to me. I'm not playing."

## Risk Management, Streaks, and Investment Process
* **Four-Asset Matrix:** Duquesne trades four asset classes—commodities, bonds, stocks, and interest rates—allowing Druckenmiller to step away from equities entirely when clarity disappears, as bonds and currencies often make their biggest moves during equity bear markets.
* **P&L Over VAR:** Druckenmiller rejects Value at Risk (VAR) and stress tests because correlations break down in chaos and bear markets (as seen in software and AI infrastructure earlier in the year). Instead, **the P&L is his true signal**: if positions aren't correlating properly, he cuts back.
* **Playing Hot and Cold Streaks:** Duquesne's 50-year track record has been built in "scoops"—grinding out 5–8% years before catching a 3–4 year run, while avoiding down calendar years. Druckenmiller sizes up when he is "seeing the ball" and makes "little bunts" when he is cold.
* **Invest and Then Investigate:** Rather than waiting for complete data, Druckenmiller makes an initial bet—big enough to hurt if wrong—using about 15% of the information a traditional investor would want, based on a chart, story, or passionate pitch. He then hands it to his research team for 2–3 weeks to decide whether to add or exit.
* **What Separates Great Investors from Good Ones:**
  * **Four Core Traits:** Unbelievable passion, intellectual curiosity, competitiveness "to the point of a sickness" (no work-life balance), and strict adherence to a personal discipline.
  * **Intellectual Humility:** Smart investors often get in their own way because high IQ breeds inflexibility. Druckenmiller's twist on Mark Twain: *"Put all your eggs in one basket and then watch the basket very carefully."*
  * **Biggest Lessons:** Open-mindedness has made him the most money; breaking his own discipline out of FOMO lost him the most (selling the Nasdaq in January 2000, then buying it back within an hour of the top 26 years ago). He also noted he can tell within the first 15 minutes if someone is a phony.

## AI Use Cases: Selling Tasks, Not Tokens
* **AI Awakening:** Druckenmiller credited a guest named Gavin (introduced via Bouzali's Zoom call a month after ChatGPT launched) for waking him up to AI being "the biggest thing in the history of American business."
* **Shifting from Infrastructure to Use Cases:** While washed-out AI infrastructure stocks may offer a tactical trade, Druckenmiller does not expect them to be the multi-year engine they were over the last four years.
* **Labs Selling Tasks:** He believes leading AI labs will stop releasing models and move away from the token business. With the world's top intelligence, they can sell tasks directly and build their own businesses—particularly in **cybersecurity** (deploying swarms of agents to defend against threats they helped create) and **healthcare**.
* **AI Bear Thesis:** When asked by Bouzali which AI bear thesis he respects most, Druckenmiller pointed to **politics and financing**.

## Quiet Structural Risks Under the Surface
* **Education and Immigration:** Druckenmiller flagged the quiet deterioration of US K–12 education, which the US has historically offset by importing global talent (estimating 8 of the top 10 tech companies are run by immigrants). He worries current immigration policy threatens to cut off that talent flow.
* **The US Deficit:** Recalling his 2011–2012 college tour warning about entitlements and demographics hitting between 2020 and 2030, Druckenmiller noted the US has continued to get away with it as the reserve currency—even after $5 trillion in COVID spending and zero interest rates—but warned of a France-like fiscal reckoning.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Economic Slowdown:** The second half of 2027 could be economically disappointing, based on commodity action and defensive stocks leading cyclicals — *Stan Druckenmiller*.
* **AI Business Model Shift:** Leading AI labs will stop selling tokens and instead sell tasks directly, building their own businesses in areas like cybersecurity and healthcare — *Stan Druckenmiller*.
* **US Fiscal Crisis & Reform:** Within the next 10 years, the US will enact fiscal reform engendered by a crisis in the financial markets — *Stan Druckenmiller*.
* **Nuclear Fusion:** Within the next 10 years, there is a 20% chance we will either have fusion or it will be clear we are going to have fusion — *Stan Druckenmiller*.
* **Space Infrastructure:** Within the next 10 years, there is at least a 70% chance we will have data centers in space — *Stan Druckenmiller*.
* **Cancer:** Within 10 years (not 20), we will beat cancer and it will become a managed disease, driven by genetic sequencing, immunotherapy, and AI — *Stan Druckenmiller*.

## Notable Quotes
> "I can't remember a period where I had less clarity on where we're going to be in 12 months." — Stan Druckenmiller

> "My own belief is that they're not going to be releasing models, and if you have the number one intelligence in the world, you can start selling tasks instead of tokens." — Stan Druckenmiller

> "Put all your eggs in one basket and then watch the basket very carefully." — Stan Druckenmiller (paraphrasing Mark Twain)

> "I think we're going to beat cancer. I think it's going to be a managed disease, and I mean in 10 years, not 20 years." — Stan Druckenmiller

items.title: Stripe CEO Patrick Collison at Silicon Valley & The World | Semafor
items.summary: Stripe CEO Patrick Collison discussed Stripe’s $7.5 billion acquisition of OpenRouter as a parallel to Stripe’s own neutral infrastructure—unifying AI tokens rather than dollars—while outlining the rise of an "AI economy" driven by agent-to-agent micropayments, the enduring value of human-made art, and the urgent need for meta-science reform.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
Stripe CEO Patrick Collison discussed Stripe’s $7.5 billion acquisition of OpenRouter as a parallel to Stripe’s own neutral infrastructure—unifying AI tokens rather than dollars—while outlining the rise of an "AI economy" driven by agent-to-agent micropayments, the enduring value of human-made art, and the urgent need for meta-science reform.

## The OpenRouter Acquisition & AI Infrastructure
* **Neutral Infrastructure Parallel:** Stripe acquired OpenRouter for $7.5 billion (roughly 6x its prior valuation) after realizing both companies share the same core mission: providing neutral, unified infrastructure for everyone from solo developers to large public companies—Stripe for dollars and payment regulations, and OpenRouter for AI tokens.
* **Hyper-Growth Metrics:** 
  * Stripe grew its revenue 41% year-over-year in the first half of the year (disclosed in an investor letter).
  * OpenRouter’s volume of tokens served grew 37% month-over-month in October.
  * Collison noted that traditional valuation multiples break down at these growth rates, making it more useful to evaluate the market equilibrium 3 to 5 years out.
* **Model Diversity & Rapid Turnover:** 
  * 73% of OpenRouter’s customer usage is for models launched within the last 60 days.
  * Developers are highly sensitive to small differences across language, image, speech recognition, and decision models, driving demand for a diverse ecosystem.
* **Open-Source & Sovereignty:** Despite geopolitical concerns around Chinese open-weight models, Collison emphasized that open-source AI is essential for customers—particularly in Europe and outside the U.S.—who require sovereignty, self-hosted inference, observability, and full-stack governance.

## Agentic Commerce & The "AI Economy"
* **Machine Payments Protocol (MPP):** Stripe launched MPP a couple of months ago alongside **Tempo**, a new blockchain protocol.
  * MPP already processes tens of thousands of machine-to-machine transactions per day, though the absolute dollar volume is currently *de minimis*.
  * Many of these transactions are settled using stablecoins.
* **Pay-at-the-Moment-of-Utility:** Rather than AI agents "going on a bender," these human-driven transactions allow software to consume usage-based APIs (e.g., weather or price data) and pay instantly at the moment of utility—eliminating the need for pre-registration, advance contracts, or billing in arrears.
* **Shift to Consumption Models:** Agentic transactions are the next logical progression in a broader internet economy shift away from traditional seat-based pricing toward usage- and consumption-based models.

## Arts, Architecture, and AI Creativity
* **New Aesthetics Initiative:** Collison and economist Tyler Cowen launched *New Aesthetics*, awarding $10,000 to $250,000 grants to artists, architects, and designers.
  * Addressing moderator Reed Albergotti’s question on why Silicon Valley lags behind older industrial hubs like Detroit in funding grand cultural institutions, Collison agreed Silicon Valley should play a much bigger role in supporting the arts.
* **Breaking the "Modernist Rut":** Collison argued that architecture has been stuck in a modernist rut for a century—noting that the Bauhaus Dessau building in Germany looks like a modern Silicon Valley office—and needs a new 21st-century aesthetic.
* **Human Art in an AI Era:** Despite being deeply AI-forward, Stripe’s publishing arms (**Stripe Press** and **Works in Progress** magazine) exclusively use human-created art. Collison argued that intentionality, purpose, and relational engagement matter to consumers, and AI-generated art would make the products worse.

## Meta-Science & Research Funding
* **Arc Institute & Policy Engagement:** Collison co-founded the Arc Institute with his wife to help academic researchers avoid "grant writing hell." He recently spoke in Washington, D.C., with Michael Kratsios (head of the Office of Science and Technology Policy) about reforming basic research grants.
* **Reviving Meta-Science:** Collison noted that "meta-science"—studying how best to fund scientists (e.g., funding projects vs. funding people) and structure institutions—has been moribund for decades. He welcomed recent policy reports calling for renewed focus on these questions, especially amid the upheaval of AI.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Agent-to-Agent Transaction Volume:** Within a few years, most transactions (by volume, though not necessarily by dollar value) will be between AI agents — *Patrick Collison (referenced by Reed Albergotti and affirmed by Collison)*.
* **Emergence of Three Economies:** Going forward, the global economy will be best understood as three distinct spheres: the non-internet economy, the internet economy, and the **AI economy** — *Patrick Collison*.
* **Endurance of Open-Source AI:** The open-source AI model ecosystem "is something that's here to stay" due to international demand for inference sovereignty — *Patrick Collison*.
* **Persistence of Human Art:** Consumer and artist preference for human-created art—caring about what humans chose to depict—will persist despite the rise of AI — *Patrick Collison*.

## Notable Quotes
> "Stripe is doing this in the realm of dollars, they're doing it in the realm of tokens, that actually there were kind of deeper commonalities than might be initially apparent." — Patrick Collison

> "Going forward, I think it might be useful to think about three economies: the non-internet economy, the internet economy, and then the AI economy." — Patrick Collison

> "I've now said something controversial that'll be clipped of that modernism is a rut, but I'll stand by it." — Patrick Collison

> "All of the art for Stripe Press and for Works in Progress is created by humans... I think people care about that fact and they want to know what humans chose to depict. It would be less interesting if it was AI art." — Patrick Collison

items.title: The Boomerang CEO(s): With MongoDB’s Dev Ittycheria
items.summary: MongoDB CEO Dev Ittycheria—who returned after a 10-month retirement following an 11-year run—breaks down the core job of a CEO into three non-negotiable pillars: setting strategy, putting the right people on the bus, and creating an environment where they can win.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
MongoDB CEO Dev Ittycheria—who returned after a 10-month retirement following an 11-year run—breaks down the core job of a CEO into three non-negotiable pillars: setting strategy, putting the right people on the bus, and creating an environment where they can win. In an era of AI-driven speed, he argues that a CEO’s toughest calls test courage rather than intelligence, requiring radical candor, fast decision-making, and a relentless hunt for bad news.

## The Three Jobs of a CEO & The Boomerang Return
* **The Core Framework:** Credited to former Palo Alto Networks CEO Mark McLaughlin, Dev Ittycheria defines the CEO role by three responsibilities; doing 997 other things well while failing at these three means failing as a CEO:
  * **Strategy:** Defining where the company is going and what it aspires to be (which changes infrequently).
  * **People:** Ensuring the right core leadership team is on the bus to execute the strategy (which requires constant assessment).
  * **Environment:** Making capital allocation decisions and building a culture ("culture as a product") that attracts, retains, and sets people up for success.
* **The Return to MongoDB:** After retiring for 10 months to spend time with family and join Sequoia, Dev received a call in Tuscany from the board chair that his successor was resigning. He returned within a week out of responsibility to MongoDB's 6,000 employees, thousands of customers, and investor base—just ahead of an Investor Day and their largest user conference in New York.
* **Immediate Restructuring:** Upon returning, Dev simplified the organization by consolidating product—which his predecessor had split into two groups—and bringing in an interim executive to cover a vacant role, aiming to eliminate ambiguity and accelerate decision-making.

## Speed, Truth, and Confrontation
* **Decision Velocity:** A company is the sum of its decisions; the best companies make good decisions quickly over a long period.
* **The Vulnerability Secret:** Dev admits his intensity can intimidate people, so he uses vulnerability—admitting his own mistakes and knowledge gaps—to create psychological safety. When leaders admit mistakes, teams mimic them, surface truth faster, and solve problems more quickly.
* **Confrontation Over Conflict Aversion:** Avoiding issues causes them to fester; if a team knows an issue exists and the CEO ignores it, the CEO becomes the problem by lowering the standard.
* **The Asymmetry of Information:** Outside the company (Glassdoor, Blind, X, Wall Street), bad news is overrepresented. Inside the company, good news finds the CEO automatically, while bad news travels slowly upward and is often sanitized. Dev assumes any bad news he hears is both late and worse than reported, so he actively hunts for it.

## Scaling Leadership & Evaluating Talent
* **Courage Over Intelligence:** Over 11 years at MongoDB, Dev went through 23 C-level executives. The hardest calls were not intellectual, but emotional—deciding to put the company ahead of loyal early executives who could not scale to the next stage.
  * **Tells of an Unscalable Exec:** Lack of self-awareness, losing their team ("you can fool people above you, sometimes around you, never below you"), and declining hiring quality.
* **What Dev Looks for in a Successor CEO:**
  * **Ownership Mindset:** Treating the business as if it is 100% of their net worth, owned for 100 years (citing Warren Buffett).
  * **Long-Term Orientation:** Avoiding myopic, transactional decisions driven by 6-to-12-month stock price targets or short-term equity triggers.
  * **People Development:** Going beyond recruiting and execution to actively coaching, giving constructive feedback, and holding people accountable.
  * **Crisis & AI Thinking:** Distinguishing "builders" from "harvesters" during downturns, and having a clear point of view on how AI impacts org design, capital allocation, and innovation.
* **Evaluating Founders & CROs:**
  * **Founders:** Brian Halligan (HubSpot CEO & Sequoia partner) and Dev debate raw compute (e.g., math Olympiad/chess prodigies) versus wisdom, taste, and judgment. Dev argues that in a world where intelligence is ubiquitous and cheap, intellectual humility, taste, and the ability to learn ("student of the game") matter more than being the "smartest kid in the class."
  * **CROs:** Dev warns against "cut-and-paste" playbooks, noting that infrastructure sales (like MongoDB's) require winning over developers, security, ops, and economic buyers, unlike many application sales. He looks for CROs who succeeded selling a second- or third-tier product against a strong incumbent rather than riding inbound demand at a market leader, and stresses conducting blind reference checks.

## Operating in the AI Era
* **What Has Changed for Modern CEOs:**
  * **Shorter Decision Half-Lives:** The world moves too fast to punt on decisions; most decisions today are two-way doors, making speed a primary weapon.
  * **Token & Unit Economics:** With compute and GPU costs, CEOs must understand gross margins and the value delivered on top of consumed tokens.
  * **Talent Density:** Companies can do much more with fewer people, placing an even higher premium on top talent.
  * **Modulating Euphoria and Panic:** Founders must keep egos in check during inbound surges (warning against COVID-style overhiring and bloat) and keep teams steady when new models drop.
* **Planning & Focus:** While running 12-month planning cycles, Dev recasts plans every 90 days to align expenses with real revenue and ruthlessly cut underperforming projects.
* **Brian Halligan’s Takeaways for HubSpot:** Returning as CEO of HubSpot, Brian is applying Dev’s advice by encouraging employees to act as if they own 100% of HubSpot shares, making faster two-way-door decisions, obsessing over leading indicators (usage, NPS, unit economics), and maintaining a steady presence between high highs and low lows.

## Notable Quotes
> "I can do a thousand things. I can do this podcast, I can go visit customers, but if I do 997 things well and these three things [strategy, people, environment] poorly, I fail as a CEO." — Dev Ittycheria

> "I think the toughest decisions I faced were not the ones that tested my intelligence, they tested my courage." — Dev Ittycheria

> "If you're not embarrassed by who you were two, three years ago, you're not growing fast enough." — Dev Ittycheria

> "Most things are two-way doors today. You can build so fast, you can change your mind on most things. So I think speed is a weapon these days." — Brian Halligan

items.title: ‘We Have To Do It’: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy On Racing China In The AI Buildout
items.summary: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy defended the company's $220 billion CapEx plan by highlighting that AWS's generative AI revenue has surpassed $25 billion in its first three years—growing 440 times faster than early AWS—and argued that the U.S. cannot afford to slow down data center construction and cede AI leadership to China.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy defended the company's $220 billion CapEx plan by highlighting that AWS's generative AI revenue has surpassed $25 billion in its first three years—growing 440 times faster than early AWS—and argued that the U.S. cannot afford to slow down data center construction and cede AI leadership to China.

## AWS AI Growth, CapEx, and Demand Signals
* **Unprecedented AI Revenue Velocity:** In response to CNBC's Kate Rooney on Wall Street's reaction to Amazon's $220 billion CapEx plan, Jassy noted that AWS's generative AI business has reached over $25 billion in annual revenue within its first three years, compared to a $57 million annual revenue run rate in AWS's first three years (~440x faster).
* **Long-Term Capacity Reservations & Backlog:**
  * Big chunks of AWS capacity are already largely reserved for 2027, much of it for 2028, and a significant portion for 2029.
  * Amazon's backlog stands at ~$580 billion, with no single company representing even 25% of it.
* **Enterprise Adoption & Barbell Demand:**
  * Over 80% of the Fortune 100 are using Bedrock, Amazon's inference service.
  * Jassy described current demand as "barbelled": AI labs consuming massive compute (e.g., ChatGPT, coding) on one end, and enterprises using AI for cost avoidance and productivity (customer service, business process automation, fraud) on the other, with core enterprise production applications in the middle still ramping up.
* **Capital Cycle & Free Cash Flow:**
  * Data centers require capital outlays ~2 years ahead of monetization, whereas servers and networking gear (the largest capital expense) are purchased just a few months ahead, giving Amazon real visibility into demand before pulling the trigger.
  * While heavy CapEx creates short-term free cash flow headwinds, Jassy expects strong long-term return on invested capital.

## Data Center Buildout, Community Impact, and US-China Competition
* **Historic Infrastructure Scale:** Jassy compared the current AI infrastructure buildout to the 1950s U.S. highway and bridge construction, noting that the country and the world had underinvested in upgrading the power grid.
* **Geopolitical Imperative:** Addressing state-level moratoriums and public backlash, Jassy warned that stopping U.S. data center construction and allowing China to establish global AI norms would be a "historic mistake" that the U.S. would regret for a long time.
* **Community Partnerships & Tax Contributions:**
  * In St. Joseph County, Indiana, Amazon will contribute over $3 billion in taxes over the next few years, compared to ~$1 million from previous landowners.
  * Through its Build Together program, Amazon has contributed another $1 billion to local neighborhood priorities.
* **Hyperscaler Capacity:** Amazon added significant capacity in 2026 and has substantially larger capacity in progress for 2027 and 2028.

## Custom Silicon, Nvidia, and AI Model Partnerships
* **Custom Silicon Scale:** Amazon's chips business—comprising Trainium (AI accelerator) and Graviton (CPU)—has surpassed a $25 billion annual revenue run rate (as of Q2). The majority of Bedrock inference runs on Trainium chips.
* **Nvidia & "Coopetition":** Jassy downplayed any impact on Amazon from recent Nvidia news, calling Nvidia and Jensen Huang a long-term, important partner alongside Amazon's own custom silicon. On export controls, Jassy stated Amazon will abide by all U.S. laws.
* **Multi-Model Strategy (Anthropic & OpenAI):**
  * Anthropic, which is set to price and list on the Nasdaq, trains models and runs inference on Trainium. Jassy dismissed "circular financing" criticisms, noting that interconnected customer-vendor relationships (like Amazon using Adobe, which runs on AWS) are standard.
  * Driven by customer demand for choice, Amazon also partnered with OpenAI to offer its models on AWS.

## Agentic Shopping and Consumer/Enterprise Health
* **Third-Party Shopping Agents:** Jassy explained that Amazon has not permanently closed amazon.com to third-party agents (like Instinct or Dots), but requires a good customer experience and a fair exchange of value.
* **Alexa for Shopping:** Over 400 million people have used Alexa for shopping in the last 12 months, driving significant downstream revenue. Jassy believes most agentic shopping will happen natively within the retailer's own app, though Amazon is in talks with horizontal agent companies.
* **Resilient Consumer & Enterprise Spending:**
  * Consumer spending has been consistent over the last 18 months, with shoppers remaining price-conscious and deal-seeking ahead of events like Amazon's "Turkey 12."
  * On the enterprise side, Jassy has seen "no attenuation" in demand, with companies resuming cloud migrations over the past 18 months.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **AWS $1 Trillion Run Rate:** AWS can become an over $1 trillion annual revenue run rate business within the next 5 to 10 years (Andy Jassy).
* **Frontier Model Landscape:** In 3 to 5 years, there will be 6 to 8 frontier models that are roughly comparable in quality—each excelling at different tasks like coding, math, reasoning, visual arts, or lower cost/latency—and one of them will be Amazon's own model (Andy Jassy).
* **Cloud Migration Flip:** Today, 80% to 85% of global IT spend is still on-premises; that equation will flip to majority cloud over the next 10 to 20 years (Andy Jassy).

## Notable Quotes
> "I cannot fathom any scenario where the United States stops building data centers and allows another country like China to establish all the norms. Like, I think that would be a historic mistake by the United States that we would all regret for a very long time." — Andy Jassy

> "We felt like when we were building AWS the last number of years, we felt like AWS could be a few hundred billion dollar revenue run rate business. We now believe it can be over a trillion dollars in the next five to 10 years." — Andy Jassy

> "Customers want choice. They don't believe in one tool to rule the world... I think three to five years from now, there are going to be six to eight models that are about as good as each other, and they're all going to be a little bit better at something." — Andy Jassy

items.title: What It Takes to Build an AI That Actually Knows You
items.summary: First Person Labs co-founder Ken Liu joins a16z’s Martin Casado and Joel de la Garza to introduce Second (available at 2.computer), a secure, portable personal context layer that continuously models your digital life—across OS events, messages, and apps—so any AI agent you choose already knows who you are without repeated prompting.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** First Person Labs co-founder Ken Liu joins a16z’s Martin Casado and Joel de la Garza to introduce **Second** (available at `2.computer`), a secure, portable personal context layer that continuously models your digital life—across OS events, messages, and apps—so any AI agent you choose already knows who you are without repeated prompting.

---

## What Second Is: The "Alfred" Model for AI Agents
* **Portable Personal Context:** Instead of re-explaining your preferences (e.g., airline seat, airport arrival time, flight class) to every new agent, **Second** builds a persistent model of your memories, priorities, goals, values, commitments, and intent.
  * You can point any agent—such as **GroqBot** or **OpenAI Codex**—to your Second so it instantly has your full work and personal context.
* **The Butler, Not the Doer:** Ken Liu frames Second using the **Alfred and Batman** analogy: Second acts as your trusted butler ("Alfred") who holds your context and interfaces with specialized external agents (e.g., shopping agents on Amazon or coding agents) on your behalf without unnecessarily exposing your identity.
* **One Second, Many Agents:** Martin Casado notes he runs multiple specialized GroqBots (for synthesizers, real estate, and family) that all interface with a single Second. Ken confirms there will not be a "third" or "fourth"—Second is designed to be your single, consistent personal data vault while ephemeral software agents spin up and down around it.

## How It Works: Tapping the OS Stream & Reflective Proactivity
* **24/7 OS-Level Event Capture:** Rather than relying solely on app connectors (like **Slack**, **Signal**, or **WhatsApp**), Second analyzes the raw, infinite stream of events your OS (**Apple**, **Microsoft**, or **Linux**) already generates—app switches, website pauses, typing patterns, and Wi-Fi connections—to hierarchically infer what you are doing.
* **Reactive vs. Reflective Proactivity:**
  * *Reactive proactivity* is simple (e.g., pinging you when an email arrives).
  * *Reflective proactivity* connects dots across long time horizons, priorities, and ongoing conversations to intervene without being asked.
  * Joel de la Garza shares an example: while planning an event with a **20% chance of weather**, his Second proactively monitored the forecast in real time and messaged him updates on whether they needed a tent.
* **Developer & Mobile Continuity:** Ken highlights "context continuity"—browsing on a laptop, switching to a phone, and having Second know your exact state up to the minute. For coding, users can simply screenshot an issue and tell their coding agent "fix," with Second supplying the full context.

## Security Architecture: Trusting an Ambient AI
* **Confidential Inference Over Policy Promises:** Joel de la Garza notes that as a self-described paranoid security veteran, he only adopted Second after reviewing its architecture. Ken explains that **Zero Data Retention (ZDR)** is merely a legal/policy promise, whereas Second supports **confidential inference**—running models inside **Nvidia** GPUs with hardware-attested confidential computing toggles so not even the provider can see inside.
* **Bring Your Own Tokens & Local Storage:**
  * Users can bring their own inference tokens (e.g., **OpenAI** or **Anthropic**) to analyze data locally on their laptop (**Second Local**).
  * For cloud-hosted backups, data is encrypted locally and only decrypted inside an attested confidential container.
* **Defending Against Prompt Injection:** When Martin asks how Second prevents another user's agent from tricking it into leaking data, Ken explains it combines deterministic rules (e.g., never retaining passwords) with LLM reasoning-based context policies (e.g., knowing Martin never messages Ken at 3:00 a.m., flagging such requests as potential impersonation).

## Economics, Model Portability, and Product Surface
* **Token Costs & Target Users:** Running 10 background agents 24/7 at 60 tokens/second costs roughly **$1,000/day** on **Opus 55**, or **$60/day** on **DeepSeek Flash**. Because of current compute costs, Second initially targets busy professionals who frequently switch tools, though Ken notes token prices have already dropped **more than 50%** since First Person Labs started.
* **Mixture of Models:** Second is built as a model-portable harness. Cheap models handle basic semantic movements (like moving a calendar invite), frontier models handle high-level weekly goal synthesis, and specialized models like **Jeff** handle fast dynamic retrieval.
* **Minimalist Product & APIs:** After early missteps trying to build custom UIs, First Person Labs stripped Second down to a minimal surface: **texting**, **API access**, and a **cloud MCP** (allowing users like Joel to talk to Second via **GroqBot audio mode** while driving). Developers and agents can build custom apps on top of Second's personal APIs (e.g., a designer friend's Second-powered app automatically knowing his preferred button placements and colors).

---

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **One Permanent Context Layer:** Personal agents will specialize and remain ephemeral, while users will maintain a single, consistent personal context store ("there will not be a third, there will not be a fourth") — *Ken Liu*
* **Confidential Inference as the Default:** Hardware-attested confidential inference will become the industry default for all personal data, replacing policy-only Zero Data Retention promises — *Ken Liu*
* **Universal Device Input:** In the long-term future, every person will have a Second, and all their devices (screens, doorbells, wearables) will simply serve as inputs and outputs for that single intelligence — *Ken Liu*
* **Cost-Driven Mass Adoption:** As token prices continue their >50% downward trajectory and models are mixed for cost efficiency, 24/7 personal context analysis will expand beyond busy professionals to general consumers — *Ken Liu*

---

## Notable Quotes
> "One of the biggest problems right now, like people have to ask, you're not supposed to ask things. They're super intelligent, but if you have a user model that just builds up by itself and then these things just keep analyzing in the background, then you can share that over instantly." — **Ken Liu**

> "I think people are very underestimating like how much the computer already knows. It's just they're sitting there, you know, waiting to be tapped, so to speak." — **Ken Liu**

> "My visions of the sci-fi future basically started when I started using Second. I'm like, finally there is something that like feels like it's got context. It feels like it knows me." — **Joel de la Garza**

> "If in the future you can have Alfred actually be an Alfred, I'll be very happy." — **Martin Casado**

items.title: Why Sam Altman and Greg Brockman Say Humans Must Stay in Control of AI
items.summary: OpenAI co-founders Sam Altman and Greg Brockman emphasized that humans must remain in control of AI's future, arguing that technical alignment and industry-wide safety standards must scale alongside rapidly advancing capabilities.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** OpenAI co-founders Sam Altman and Greg Brockman emphasized that humans must remain in control of AI's future, arguing that technical alignment and industry-wide safety standards must scale alongside rapidly advancing capabilities. Alongside detailing massive commercial momentum—including 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users and 70% annualized Q3 revenue growth—they outlined OpenAI's push toward vertical integration with its own data centers and upcoming "Jalapeno" inference chip.

## Human Control, Alignment, and Safety
* **Rejecting the AI Handover:** Both Sam Altman and Greg Brockman strongly opposed Silicon Valley narratives suggesting a gradual handover of control to AI, insisting humans must retain agency over the future.
  * **Disagreement with Microsoft:** Altman pushed back against Satya Nadella’s recent claim that AI models cannot be aligned and must instead be contained, arguing alignment is technically achievable even though the bar for confidence must rise with model capabilities.
  * **Degrading Monitoring:** Brockman noted that traditional "chain of thought" monitoring is degrading because newer models can perform more reasoning within a single forward pass without writing out their thinking, requiring new technical monitoring approaches.
* **Shift to Development Safety:** Brockman explained that AI has transitioned from needing *deployment* safety to requiring *development* safety, as models are now capable enough to have real-world interactions during training.
  * **August Security Sprint:** Following an August security incident involving Hugging Face, Brockman led a sprint that paused 25% of OpenAI's production engineering projects to focus engineers on securing the company using its own frontier cyber models.
  * **Iterative Deployment Defense:** Addressing a California Attorney General lawsuit alleging OpenAI knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight, Altman rejected the characterization, stating that confronting reality through iterative deployment is the only way to make the technology safe.
* **Industry-Wide Standards:** Altman warned against a "race dynamic in the fog of war" among competing labs, calling for shared safety standards and greater transparency.
  * **Anthropic IPO:** Explaining his *Fortune* magazine comment that going public right now is ill-advised given current safety challenges, Altman said OpenAI plans to go public eventually but must currently navigate complex tradeoffs between commercial viability and security.

## Business Momentum, Compute, and Vertical Integration
* **User and Revenue Scale:** Brockman shared several concrete metrics demonstrating OpenAI's commercial growth:
  * **ChatGPT Reach:** Over 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT weekly, including 330 million people using it for health queries every week.
  * **Q3 Financials:** OpenAI's Q3 topline revenue grew 70% annualized, and enterprise revenue doubled in Q3 alone.
* **The Compute Bottleneck:** Brockman stated that the world is not building enough compute and confirmed he has personally asked both Elon Musk and Sergey Brin for additional compute capacity.
* **Vertical Integration & Chip Design:** Altman noted OpenAI is the only company building the entire intelligence stack—from consumer and enterprise platforms to data centers and custom silicon.
  * **Jalapeno Chip:** Brockman highlighted OpenAI's upcoming custom inference chip, "Jalapeno," stating it is designed to optimize the Pareto curve of peak intelligence and price efficiency.
  * **AMD Partnership:** Brockman announced that working with AMD, OpenAI models achieved a full year's worth of generational chip design improvements in just five months.
  * **High-Compute Use Cases:** Brockman cited applying $1 million worth of compute to find 1,000 bugs in the Linux kernel in a short period with a single researcher (compared to the ~20 bugs typically found per year).
  * **Cost Efficiency:** Addressing Microsoft's claim that it can run AI tasks at 5% of OpenAI's cost, Altman welcomed the competition, stating OpenAI wants to drive down costs so everyone can use more AI.

## Leadership Partnership, Governance, and External Pressures
* **11-Year Partnership:** Brockman traced their dynamic back to a July 2015 dinner, describing a high-bandwidth partnership built on rapid-fire communication (5–6 short calls a day early on) and a willingness to "disagree and commit" on major strategic questions.
* **Equity and Control:** Addressing the disparity between Brockman’s ~$30 billion equity stake and Altman’s lack of equity, Brockman noted he originally advocated for Altman to take equity, and Altman admitted, "I should have listened to Greg."
  * **Governance Structure:** Brockman pointed out that OpenAI is the only major AI company where the founders do not hold supermajority control.
* **Legal and Public Scrutiny:**
  * **Jensen Huang / NVIDIA:** Both expressed personal support for NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang amid his recent challenges, calling him "singular" and noting NVIDIA's foundational bet on OpenAI.
  * **White House Accord:** Brockman expressed alignment with the White House Accord on AI safety standards.
  * **NYT Litigation:** Asked about internal emails regarding scraping *The New York Times* past its paywall, Brockman declined to comment due to active litigation, noting he had already addressed it in his deposition.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Alignment Progress:** "I expect we will have continued progress [on alignment] and I think our ability to push capabilities forward will be dependent on us having that progress." — *Sam Altman*
* **OpenAI IPO:** OpenAI plans to become a public company "at some point." — *Sam Altman*
* **Custom Silicon:** "We have our own chip coming, Jalapeno, which is I think going to be the best inference chip in the industry." — *Greg Brockman*
* **Economic Acceleration:** "I think that the economy again is going to be massively accelerated through this technology. I think that the biggest thing, the biggest limiter, really just will be compute." — *Greg Brockman*

## Notable Quotes
> "I don't want to be a Labrador. I don't want my kids to be Labradors. I want people to have the agency over the future that we have had." — *Sam Altman*

> "If the world and the companies developing AI treated the next four years like they've treated the last four years, I think that would be very bad." — *Sam Altman*

> "We're now at a point where development safety... that the models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment. That's new." — *Greg Brockman*

items.title: Bill Ackman Outlines The Activist Playbook To Reinstate Jensen Huang | Silicon Valley & The World
items.summary: At Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, billionaire activist investor Bill Ackman outlined how he would theoretically run a campaign to reinstate ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—though he noted his direct involvement is "unlikely."
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
At Semafor’s *Silicon Valley & The World*, billionaire activist investor Bill Ackman outlined how he would theoretically run a campaign to reinstate ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—though he noted his direct involvement is "unlikely." Alongside the President’s chief technology advisor (referred to as "Director"), Ackman also discussed the rise of founder-controlled public companies, U.S. AI export controls, and how commercial instincts and AI are reshaping scientific philanthropy.

## The Activist Playbook for Reinstating Jensen Huang
* **Ackman’s Defense:** Bill Ackman rushed to Huang’s defense out of a belief in "innocent until proven guilty" and a favorable past relationship with Huang, noting that the best time to help someone is when they are down.
* **Likelihood of Involvement:** Ackman said it is "unlikely" he will get directly involved, though he called it a "pretty interesting activist setup" with "Steve Jobsian" elements that would likely garner significant shareholder support.
* **Tactical Execution:** 
  * Establish the facts first to resolve current legal uncertainties; if Huang’s missteps were a "personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy," there is a strong case for reinstatement.
  * Partner with Huang, who owns 3% of Nvidia, to call a special shareholder meeting.
  * Present the facts and propose board changes—Ackman expects "the writing will be on the wall very quickly," forcing the board to reinstate Huang before a vote even occurs.
* **Board Ethics on Lying:** While "truth is pretty darn important" between a board and a CEO, Ackman distinguished between a lie regarding a personal relationship versus a lie about next quarter's revenue or core business operations.

## Founder Control & Public Market Short-Termism
* **The Rise of the "Golden Share":** Moderator Liz Hoffman noted that Anthropic is going public this week with a structure giving its seven cofounders a "golden share" that controls nearly everything at the company.
* **The Case for Founder Control:** Ackman argued that founder-led companies historically create far more long-term value than dispersed-ownership companies run by hired CEOs, though he cautioned against blindly passing that golden share to the "next generation."
* **Wall Street Short-Termism:** 
  * Index funds—which Ackman described as automated, passive entities operating for basis points rather than "real owners"—now own 25% of corporate America.
  * Combined with quantitative trading, options, and 3x levered ETFs, public markets force short-term thinking, making founder control or large, long-term anchor investors increasingly logical.

## U.S. Tech Stack, Export Controls & Security
* **Exporting the U.S. Stack:** The Director emphasized that winning in superintelligence (SI) requires U.S. companies to have the chips they need, while also sharing a trusted Western tech stack globally via the **American SI Export Program** (created by executive order in July of last year).
* **Chip Diversion & Enforcement:** Addressing tensions over Nvidia's chip sales, the Director pointed to new Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) rules announced today regarding remote chip access and licensing requirements for certain countries.
* **Workforce & IP Security:** With young AI companies growing rapidly, the Director urged CEOs to take security seriously and protect frontier model weights—calling them some of the most valuable assets in the world.

## AI in Science & Reforming Philanthropy
* **Ackman’s AI-Native Brain Institute:** Ackman and his wife are endowing a Brain Institute in New York (initially $400M, now closer to $800M). Operating in "super-founder mode," Ackman’s first hires include a Chief AI Officer, and he previously connected Huang’s healthcare team with Mount Sinai’s brain data.
* **Free Market Over Mandates:** Both Ackman and the Director rejected the idea of forcing AI labs to devote 25% of their compute to curing cancer or brain disease.
* **SI for Science Momentum:** 
  * The Director highlighted that philanthropic organizations like the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub and Patrick Collison’s Arc Institute are investing hundreds of millions to billions into SI-powered science.
  * A month ago, the administration hosted an "SI for Science" event announcing **$2.4 billion** in donations from the SI community to provide free compute to American scientists.
  * Roughly a quarter of OpenAI (nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars) and similar commitments from Anthropic's founders are earmarked for philanthropic endeavors.
* **Applying Commercial Instincts to Nonprofits:** 
  * Having given away **$1.5 billion** over 20 years through the Pershing Square Foundation, Ackman criticized traditional philanthropy for enormous waste, lack of M&A, and lack of equity compensation.
  * His Brain Institute will operate with commercial instincts: creating and monetizing IP through company formation, sharing equity with employees, and utilizing a captive venture fund (which has already invested **$90 million** in brain-computer interface and device companies) to funnel returns back into the institute.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **On Nvidia Governance:** If an activist partners with Jensen Huang (3% owner) to call a special meeting, "the writing will be on the wall very quickly... at which point you don't even have to go to the meeting, you just put him back in." — *Bill Ackman*
* **On Scientific Discovery:** "SI is going to transform entirely the way that scientists do their work from material science, to chemistry, to math, to physics, to biochemistry, to the way the pharmaceuticals are developed." — *Director (President's Chief Technology Advisor)*
* **On Philanthropic Capital:** "There's going to be more money moving into the SI for Science field than we could ever imagine." — *Director (President's Chief Technology Advisor)*

## Notable Quotes
> "If it's a personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy, I think there's a very powerful case for putting him back in place." — *Bill Ackman, on Jensen Huang*

> "More and more of American companies are being controlled by automated machines that operate for basis points and own 25% of corporate America... it's not a world in which owners behave like owners, except for a very small handful of more active owners and founders." — *Bill Ackman*

> "You don't have to be an expert in this to understand how important the weights are to these frontier models. These are some of the most important and most valuable assets in the entire world, and they should be rightfully protected." — *Director (President's Chief Technology Advisor)*

> "People have created a lot more value for the world with for-profit companies than they have with nonprofits, but there are gaps in the capital markets where nonprofits can step in and accomplish things." — *Bill Ackman*

items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi argues that while AGI is already here, enterprises are stuck using AI as a glorified Google search due to context, security, cost, and IP sovereignty bottlenecks. He demonstrates how Databricks uses its internal "Genie" ontology to run the company like "management Moneyball," explains why Databricks is staying private for now, and dismisses AI doom scenarios because none of the four conditions for recursive self-improvement (RSI) are currently met.

---

## Databricks' Origin & Contrarian Bets
- **UC Berkeley Roots:** Founded in 2013 out of UC Berkeley's AMPlab (~20 researchers, the largest AI lab at the time), where Ali Ghodsi and his team worked on the 2008–2009 Netflix Prize ($1M for a 10% improvement in movie recommendations). "AMP" stood for Algorithms, Machine Learning, and People—reflecting an early belief in human-in-the-loop AI.
- **Three Contrarian Bets:** At a time when AI was dismissed as niche ad-tech, Databricks bet everything on:
  - **Cloud:** Separating compute and storage (an analyst firm bet Ali it would be a "strategic blunder" that would sink the company).
  - **AI Use Cases:** Building for enterprise data science teams.
  - **Open Source:** Making the core technology open.
- **Scale & Growth:** Grew from $1.5M in revenue in 2015 to a $7B+ run rate by August 2026, growing 70–80% YoY (with Ali aiming for >100% growth) across a 12,000-person organization.

## AGI Is Here, But Enterprise AI Is Behind
- **AGI vs. Superintelligence:** Ghodsi believes AGI—as defined by AMPlab in 2009–2010—was achieved last year, though researchers have moved the goalpost. By contrast, **Superintelligence** (Nick Bostrom's 2014 definition: doing 1,000 years of human thought in a minute) remains the obsession of frontier labs.
- **Current Enterprise Reality:** Global 2000 and Fortune 500 companies mostly use AI as a "glorified Google search" (chatbots) and for coding (seeing 20–30% speedups), rather than running thousands of autonomous agents.
- **Four Bottlenecks Holding Enterprises Back:**
  - **The Context Problem:** AI is useless if it isn't in the room. One major bank CEO told Ghodsi they will "never" record meetings due to liability.
  - **Cybersecurity & Surface Area:** Connecting agents to all corporate data multiplies attack surface area by 1,000x+ and creates insider threat risks.
  - **Exponential Token Costs:** Token spend rises exponentially without a matching exponential lift in revenue, prompting CFOs to push back on OpEx and COGS.
  - **Data & Intelligence Sovereignty:** Companies fear IP leakage into foundation model providers (e.g., Anthropic, OpenAI) that release competing features every two weeks.
- **Digital Natives Lead:** Younger companies (10–15 years old), such as Jack Dorsey's Block/Square (building a "Company World Model"), are far ahead of 20–50-year-old legacy enterprises.

## Live Demo: "Genie" & Management Moneyball
- **The Company Ontology:** Databricks' **Genie** product constructs a live, 24/7 graph of the entire company—mapping org charts, emails, Slack, docs, spreadsheets, and meeting transcripts—to cut latency across hierarchical org charts.
- **HR Survey & Causality:** Out of 10,000+ employee responses, executive leadership scored 88%, work-life balance 60%, and "action" (feeling heard) ~33%. When the CFO hypothesized that poor work-life blend caused low action, Genie disproved causality (e.g., surfacing a manager with 44% work-life blend and 77% action) and sliced root causes by department (PM: too many stakeholders; Engineering: tools/systems; Sales Ops: career growth).
- **Engineering Productivity (The L-Curve):** Plotting weekly pull requests across 2,000 engineers revealed an L-shape where the top 10% ship vastly more code by running "automated factories." Overlaying token cost showed top shippers weren't necessarily spending more because they route simpler tasks to open-source/cheaper models.
- **Eliminating Human Blockers:** Genie tracks "human blockers" (legal, finance, sibling orgs) and audits whether regional offices (e.g., Japan vs. EMEA vs. LatAm) adhere to core cultural principles. Jason Calacanis noted he built a similar internal bot ("Major Decisions") to track Slack, Notion, and email for decision-making speed.

## Staying Private vs. Going Public
- **The Case for Going Public:** Provides access to public capital, massive quarterly marketing events, and liquid M&A currency (though Databricks has already executed $1B+ acquisitions privately).
- **Why Databricks Is Staying Private (For Now):**
  - **Avoiding the Public Rollercoaster:** Ghodsi wants to shield employees from public market sentiment swings during the AI transition, where a sudden stock drop feels like a pay cut and triggers attrition.
  - **Vibrant Secondary Liquidity:** Databricks has raised $20B–$30B in annual tender offers. Employees rarely use up the full tender allocation because they prefer to hold onto 70–80% compounding growth.

## RSI, Cyber Risk & The Doom Debate
- **Why We Don't Have RSI:** Writing 98% of code with AI does not equal Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). Ghodsi outlines **four unmet conditions** required for an RSI flywheel:
  1. *Faster Training:* Next-gen models must train super-linearly faster (currently, pre-training takes longer and follows scaling laws requiring exponentially more hardware).
  2. *Fewer Resources:* Training must use less compute, not 10x more hardware each generation.
  3. *Generalized Accuracy:* Accuracy must improve at least linearly across all domains, not just in narrow RL gyms or math.
  4. *Continuous Loop:* All three must compound continuously (e.g., training dropping from 3 months → 1 month → 2 weeks → 1 week, and cost dropping from $100M → $50M → $1M).
- **Cyber Risk Is Real, But Finite:** Cyber is asymmetric—attackers only need 1 success out of thousands of agents, while defenders must be 100% secure. Databricks addresses this with **Lakewatch**. However, code vulnerabilities are finite; as AI scans new code and rewrites/shadow-patches legacy code, software will reach a more secure steady state.
- **Tangible AI Wins:** Regeneron used Databricks to identify the genome behind chronic liver disease; Merck and Databricks trained **Teddy** (Transformer Enabled Drug Discovery) on gene regulatory networks (GRN); Crisis Textline uses LLMs to detect self-harm; and Zipline uses Databricks for drone delivery operations.

---

## Predictions & Forward Calls
- **Slow Enterprise & GDP Rollout:** Solving the enterprise context gap and seeing broad GDP impact from AI will take **10–15 years** (a decade+), rather than the 6–24 months predicted by frontier labs — *Ali Ghodsi*
- **Historic Code Volume:** In **less than the next 12 months**, humanity will write more code than ever in history, and it will be secure thanks to AI vulnerability scanning — *Ali Ghodsi*
- **Databricks IPO:** Databricks **will go public** eventually, though not during the current AI transition period — *Ali Ghodsi*
- **AI Extinction Risk:** The probability of a 10% chance that 7 billion people die from AI is **close to zero** — *Ali Ghodsi*

---

## Notable Quotes
> "If you stop all progress right now, I think we have all the intelligence we need to completely transform the planet." — *Ali Ghodsi*

> "Just because 98% of the code is being written by AI, we don't have RSI. If it automates the last 2%, who cares?" — *Ali Ghodsi*

> "We're actually getting into like management Moneyball, aren't we?" — *Jason Calacanis*

> "I actually think GDP will move very slowly, and it's going to take decades." — *Ali Ghodsi*

items.title: Dylan Patel, SemiAnalysis
items.summary: Dylan Patel is expanding SemiAnalysis into a research and investment empire—spanning 115 employees, the acquisition of Citrini Research, and a new $500 million hardware-focused venture fund—while tracking major shifts in AI, including multi-gigawatt data center permitting delays and a market transition where product execution (like Meta’s Muse and Perplexity) is outperforming raw foundation model labs.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
Dylan Patel is expanding SemiAnalysis into a research and investment empire—spanning 115 employees, the acquisition of Citrini Research, and a new $500 million hardware-focused venture fund—while tracking major shifts in AI, including multi-gigawatt data center permitting delays and a market transition where product execution (like Meta’s Muse and Perplexity) is outperforming raw foundation model labs.

## Data Center Bottlenecks, Regulation & Public Perception
* **Permitting Delays Over Supply Chain:** SemiAnalysis has pushed back multiple gigawatts of data center capacity from 2027 into 2028, and pushed several gigawatts out of 2028 entirely—not due to labor or equipment shortages, but because permits are unavailable.
* **Texas Regulatory Landscape:** Governor Hinojosa in Texas has been constructive, signaling she will not stop data centers as long as they do not raise electricity prices and are reasonable stewards of water.
  * However, she holds significant leverage via water, wastewater, stormwater, and air permits (which can even stop off-grid data centers).
  * A potential sticking point is union labor mandates, as Texas has very little union labor and non-union electricians and industrial plumbers on data center sites already make $200,000+ per year.
* **Public Ignorance vs. Sentiment:** A poll conducted by SemiAnalysis and David Shor across counties with 100MW+ data centers revealed that **49%** of residents did not even know a data center was in their county. In counties with a 100MW+ data center planned in the next three years, only **40%** knew it was coming.
  * Most local opposition stems from nebulous anti-AI sentiment online rather than actual local impact, though poorly executed projects can be loud or fail to return tax value.
  * Conversely, well-structured projects generate massive local revenue—such as a county in Louisiana that paid all its teachers $20,000 bonuses from data center property taxes. Patel notes companies can easily buy goodwill by subsidizing power for everyone within a 30-mile radius.
* **The Water Usage Myth:** Patel debunked exaggerated water narratives (citing a *New York Times* bestseller that overestimated data center water usage by 1,000x), noting that all of Elon Musk’s data centers use less embedded water than **three In-N-Out** restaurants when accounting for the agricultural supply chain of beef versus chip fabs and power generation.

## The AI Race: Models vs. Products
* **Lab Competition:** Responding to host Molly O'Shea’s framing of the "Four Seasons of AI" (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX), Patel noted that markets smooth out valuations rather than swinging wildly on single releases. Anthropic dominated Q2, OpenAI dominated Q3, and Anthropic is back ahead with Opus 3.5 and Fable 5.2 while OpenAI delays model releases.
* **Product Execution Beats Raw Models:** Patel argued that OpenAI and Anthropic are bad at building products. Meta’s **Muse** (beta-tested by Patel) and **Instinct** (which primarily uses open models) are vastly superior products compared to OpenAI’s **Dots** or Codex, which are crippled by overzealous safety filters ("Guardian"). He also criticized OpenAI’s chat app UI as confusing for a billion-user app.
* **SemiAnalysis’s $15M AI Spend:** SemiAnalysis spends **$15 million per year** on AI. Over the last few months, its spend on persistent agents jumped from 0% to **45%**—with the vast majority flowing through **Perplexity** (which acts as a better harness over Claude and OpenAI on the backend) rather than Anthropic’s Claude tags or OpenAI’s Dots.
* **Enterprise Stickiness & Startup Viability:** While developer tools like CloudCode and Codex are easy to switch away from, enterprise contracts are becoming sticky (e.g., Anthropic offering discounts if **70%+** of an enterprise's AI spend is with them). Among application startups, Patel believes most will fail, though **Instinct**, **Sierra**, and **Harvey** are showing real revenue growth and staying power (even as Harvey’s margins seesaw).

## Building the SemiAnalysis Empire & $500M VC Fund
* **Global Footprint & Business Model:** SemiAnalysis now employs **115 people** across **15 countries** (with offices in New York, Chicago, SF, Oregon, Singapore, and Korea). Its core revenue comes from selling proprietary datasets (tracking every data center, chip, and supply chain metric globally) and one-on-one consulting for hyperscalers, semiconductor firms, and AI labs.
* **Acquiring Citrini Research:** Patel acquired Citrini Research (led by James and director of research Kyle) to help operationalize their business. Citrini remains a completely separate company with full editorial independence—even when their macro/AI calls turn bearish, contrasting with Patel’s long-term bullishness.
* **$500M Solo GP Venture Fund:** Patel raised a **$500 million** early-stage (Seed/Series A) venture fund as a solo GP, focusing on hardware, infrastructure, silicon, optics, manufacturing, networking, and robotics—areas where SemiAnalysis’s deep technical bench (former ASML, TSMC, Intel, Nvidia, and hyperscaler engineers) gives him an edge.
* **Strict Independence & Firewalls:** The fund is legally firewalled from SemiAnalysis and Citrini. Patel refuses to take paid partnerships or ads, and maintains strict objectivity—publicly criticizing his biggest customers (e.g., calling out Nvidia’s anti-competitive practices with neoclouds) and even his own portfolio companies (e.g., publicly noting Fluidstack’s data center delays, or critiquing Iris Energy/IREN’s unreliable cloud tech while acknowledging the value of their powered land).

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Space Data Centers:** Engineering data centers in space is extremely difficult and will not solve capacity constraints in the next 3–4 years. While Elon Musk is aiming for 2028, Patel "takes the over" on that timeline, predicting **1 gigawatt in space** sometime this decade (around **2030**) — *Dylan Patel*.
* **Hardware Innovation Acceleration:** Within **1 year**, the number of companies building hardware—and doing it well—will skyrocket, driven by AI models improving on complex technical benchmarks like SemiAnalysis’s new **GDPX** (which tests cyber, chip design, hardware design, material science, bio, and quant RSI) — *Dylan Patel*.
* **Startup Attrition:** Most AI application startups will fail, though select companies with strong product-market fit and revenue velocity (such as Instinct, Sierra, and Harvey) will achieve long-term staying power — *Dylan Patel*.

## Notable Quotes
> "49% of people in counties that have a 100-megawatt data center did not even know there was a data center in their county." — Dylan Patel

> "All of Elon Musk's data centers use less water than three In-N-Outs... if you count the supply chain of cows." — Dylan Patel

> "Over the last few months, we've gone from zero persistent agents to 45% of our $15 million a year AI spend being persistent agents. And that 45%, the vast majority of it is not through Anthropic's Claude tags or OpenAI's Slack agent or Dots... it's through Perplexity." — Dylan Patel

> "Just because you're invested in something, or you have financial interest, doesn't mean you have to just be the tail that's wagged by the dog." — Dylan Patel

items.title: Giving Every Kid a Stake in Capitalism | Brad Gerstner & Geoffrey Canada
items.summary: Passed on July 4, 2025, the Invest America Act automatically opens universal capital accounts (530A / "Trump accounts") for every American child—70 million accounts are already open—seeding $1,000 in the S&P 500 at birth and unlocking a "Giving Pledge 2.0" wave of direct philanthropy from donors like Michael Dell and Elon Musk.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Passed on July 4, 2025, the Invest America Act automatically opens universal capital accounts (530A / "Trump accounts") for every American child—70 million accounts are already open—seeding $1,000 in the S&P 500 at birth and unlocking a "Giving Pledge 2.0" wave of direct philanthropy from donors like Michael Dell and Elon Musk. Brad Gerstner and Geoffrey Canada argue that giving every kid a stake in capitalism is the essential social contract for the AI age, solving the distribution problem that education alone cannot fix.

## The Capital Gap & Social Unrest
*   **Education Isn't Enough Without Capital:** Geoffrey Canada (Founder, Harlem Children's Zone) noted that despite graduating over 2,000 kids with college degrees (with ~1,000 currently in college), a single $500–$1,500 emergency can still bankrupt them.
    *   Earlier efforts like the 2009 Seed program and HCZ CEO Kwame Osei-Kessy's 2021 "Wealth Build" initiative (which raised over $100 million) proved the concept, but lacked national scale.
*   **The Ticking Time Bomb:** Canada warned that when parents sacrifice their health and their kids still fall behind, the system breeds revolt—citing 1960s riots, Raj Chetty's research on the fading American Dream, and modern protests in London, Paris, and Spain (4 million protesters).
    *   He emphasized this is not just an inner-city issue, but an economic crisis affecting poor white communities just as deeply.
*   **Capitalism Without Capital:** Brad Gerstner (Founder & CEO, Altimeter Capital) pointed out that less than half of Americans under age 40 believe in capitalism simply because they have no capital.

## How Invest America (530A) Accounts Work
*   **Automatic & Universal:** Signed into law on July 4, 2025, the Treasury Department automatically opens a 530A account for all 3.7 million babies born annually (10,000 per day) with $1,000 invested in the S&P 500.
    *   Every American child under 18 was grandfathered in, resulting in 70 million accounts already open.
*   **Product Design & Ownership:** Parents simply download an app to claim the account; there is no cash and no investment decisions, as all funds sweep automatically into the S&P 500.
    *   To make compounding tangible, the app displays look-through ownership of underlying companies like Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, and Walmart, and includes an easy QR code/Apple Pay button for $5–$10 contributions.
    *   At age 18, recipients can withdraw up to 25% for a home, business, college, or trade, while the remainder rolls into an IRA.
*   **Economic Impact:** A Milken Institute study by Rob Shapiro and Kevin Hassett found universal capital accounts increase high school/college graduation, homeownership, business creation, and taxpaying rates, while reducing incarceration.

## Giving Pledge 2.0: Direct Philanthropy at Scale
*   **Eliminating Friction:** Patrick O'Shaughnessy highlighted that the original Giving Pledge lacked tangible, direct impact. The new accounts create a direct-giving platform via a one-page agreement with the U.S. Treasury.
*   **Major Commitments:**
    *   **Michael & Susan Dell:** Contributed $6.25 billion ($250 each to 25 million kids aged 2–10 in the bottom 75% of zip codes).
    *   **Elon Musk & SpaceX:** Musk pledged 1 share of SpaceX to all 70 million kids (an $11.5 billion gift), while SpaceX CEO Gwynne Shotwell is giving 2 million shares to kids aged 10–18 in the bottom 50% of income zip codes.
    *   **Regional & Corporate Donors:** Gerstner funded $250 for every child under 5 in Indiana's bottom zip codes and $250 each for 3,000 kids at a Bronx school; Ray Dalio (CT), Frank Slootman (MT), and Neal Mehta ($100 per kid in San Francisco) have joined, and Anthropic announced its philanthropic arm will fund direct citizen accounts.

## Overcoming Diffusion, Political, & Education Hurdles
*   **The "Free Money" Scam Perception:** Canada stressed that poor families often assume free money is a scam. HCZ, Robin Hood, and NYC teachers will push parents to claim accounts on the first day of kindergarten.
*   **Bipartisan Politics & Branding:** While the "Trump accounts" moniker alienates some Democrats—similar to early GOP resistance to "Obamacare"—the policy has broad bipartisan backing (including Presidents Clinton and Obama, Governors Gavin Newsom and Wes Moore, Senator Cory Booker, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent).
    *   Account creation is permanent, though the $1,000 birth grant is funded through 2029 and requires Congressional reauthorization every four years.
    *   Gerstner urged Newsom to block-grant California's $200 million Cal Kids program directly into 530A accounts to consolidate fragmented state efforts.
*   **Financial Literacy:** HCZ acquired an ed-tech company to teach parents and kids about compounding. Texas has already deployed a curriculum around these accounts for 500,000 students, 38 states mandate financial literacy, and AI tutors (via OpenAI/Anthropic) will be embedded directly in the app.

## AI, Keynes's Forecast, & The New Social Contract
*   **Sharing AI's Upside:** Canada noted that young people mostly hear that AI will eliminate their jobs or pose existential risks; giving them equity in companies like SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic ensures they share in the reward, not just the risk.
*   **Keynes's 1930 Parallel:** Gerstner cited John Maynard Keynes's 1930 essay *"Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren"*—written during 22% unemployment (vs. 4.1% today)—which coined "technological unemployment" and predicted living standards would rise 4x–8x in 100 years (by 2030, the economy is 8.2x larger, and 80% of today's jobs didn't exist in 1930).
*   **1935 vs. 2025:** Just as the 1935 Social Security Act created a social contract for the industrial age to protect *labor*, the 2025 Invest America Act creates the social contract for the AI age by giving every citizen *capital*.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
*   "In just a few months, every one of those [70 million] accounts will have money in it." — Brad Gerstner
*   "Over the next 10 to 15 years, we will have $3 to $5 trillion dollars in these accounts." — Brad Gerstner
*   "The $25 trillion dollars of wealth in the United States that's going to change hands over the course of the next 10 to 15 years, you're going to see 10 or 20% of that go directly into these kids' accounts." — Brad Gerstner
*   "I'm highly confident that [making the $1,000 at birth permanent] will get done. I think that could even get done in this lame duck session." — Brad Gerstner

## Notable Quotes
> "There is no capitalism without capital." — Brad Gerstner

> "You can have a great education. You have no money. You are literally one emergency away from bankruptcy." — Geoffrey Canada

> "We do not have an abundance problem. We do not have an invention problem. We have a distribution problem." — Brad Gerstner

> "I wasn't down with capitalism until I got some capital." — Geoffrey Canada

items.title: How One Piece Of Advice Helped Remitly’s Founder Build A $4.6 Billion FinTech Giant
items.summary: A single piece of advice from Harvard Business School professor Nittin Noria—to take "the road less traveled" by leaving Barkley's London headquarters for Nairobi, Kenya—led Matt Oppenheimer to discover the broken cross-border payments system and build Remitly into a $4.6 billion FinTech giant processing $75 billion annually across 175+ countries.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** A single piece of advice from Harvard Business School professor Nittin Noria—to take "the road less traveled" by leaving Barkley's London headquarters for Nairobi, Kenya—led Matt Oppenheimer to discover the broken cross-border payments system and build Remitly into a $4.6 billion FinTech giant processing $75 billion annually across 175+ countries.

## The Advice That Sparked Remitly
* **The Mentor:** Nittin Noria, Oppenheimer's professor in Harvard Business School's *Authentic Leadership Development* class (originally started by Bill George) and later Dean of HBS, gave Oppenheimer career-altering advice after business school.
